title: Field closure, ice neurons, and when a dendrite is a motif
summary: Dendritic silhouettes are cheap. Pond ice neurons, diffusion-limited aggregates, wiring-minimizing arbors, and biological neurons can share a branching statistic because they share a growth instability, not because they are functionally similar. We take that observation as a modeling constraint. The ice neuron only structurally resembles a biological neuron. A biological neuron carries an internal state and a field that it helps generate, letting geometry, dynamics, and field co-sculpt one another. In our construction, the ice neuron is the zero-gain limit of an interfacial system in which a FitzHugh--Nagumo state lives on the moving front and writes back into the field that drives it, with dimensionless gain $γ$. At $γ=0$, morphology and internal dynamics decouple into a Mullins--Sekerka growth band and a damped oscillator. Finite $γ$ deforms the spectrum, shifts the selected instability, and opens an oscillatory region below the isolated Hopf threshold. On a dendrite grown at $γ=0$ and then frozen, field closure increases distal persistence without changing the geometry; its first-order effect remains positive across repeated realizations of the same growth rule and localizes to a small set of non-cable field shortcuts. Nonlinear dynamics remain finite beyond the linear instability: below threshold, closure is almost the transmission; at spike amplitude, it is a correction to a regenerative cable event. A dendritic tree therefore is not intrinsically a structural spandrel. Shape alone is morphology without an internal state or a source term. That is the dendritic silhouette of the ice neuron. Excitability adds an active cable. Field closure is the biophysical mélange in which the neuron helps write the field that acts back on it, sculpting its dynamics and, during growth, its structure. That is a biological neuron.

AI.tldr: The paper argues dendritic morphology alone is insufficient; a biological neuron requires an internal state and a self-generated field. Using a FitzHugh–Nagumo state on a growing front (gain γ), it shows that closing the field loop reshapes dynamics and structure, with measurable effects on distal persistence and oscillations.
AI.motivation: Branching statistics are shared across unrelated systems (ice neurons, DLA, biological neurons) because of a common growth instability, not functional similarity. The authors treat this as a modeling warning: structural resemblance ("shape alone") does not imply a biological neuron. They aim to identify the minimal ingredients beyond geometry that make a neuron biological.
AI.method: An interfacial growth system where a FitzHugh–Nagumo state lives on the moving front and writes back into the driving field, with dimensionless gain γ. γ=0 gives the "ice neuron" limit, decoupling morphology (Mullins–Sekerka band) from dynamics (damped oscillator). Finite γ deforms the spectrum, shifts the selected instability, and opens an oscillatory region below the isolated Hopf threshold. Field closure is tested on dendrites grown at γ=0 and frozen.
AI.result: At γ=0 morphology and dynamics decouple. Finite γ shifts the instability and creates sub-Hopf oscillations. Field closure increases distal persistence without changing geometry, is robustly positive across realizations, and localizes to a few non-cable field shortcuts. Below threshold, closure nearly equals transmission; at spike amplitude it is only a correction to a regenerative cable event. Nonlinear dynamics remain finite beyond the linear instability.
AI.conclusion: A dendritic tree is not intrinsically a structural spandrel. Shape alone is the "ice neuron": morphology without internal state or source term. Biological excitability adds an active cable, and field closure—the biophysical mélange where the neuron writes the field that acts back on it—sculpts both its dynamics and, during growth, its structure. That is a biological neuron.

title: Improving scoring functions for protein-protein docking with LambdaLoss
summary: Modeling protein-protein interactions requires accurate scoring functions that can rank potential poses (conformations) of a protein-protein complex to differentiate near-native poses from incorrect ones. Here, we propose a general framework for improving protein-protein pose ranking and other biomolecular interaction models using the LambdaLoss loss function from the Learning-to-Rank field. We test this framework by fine-tuning the energy prediction head of DFMDock with the LambdaLoss on an augmented dataset of 2.9M decoy poses derived from the DIPS dataset. On targets from the CAPRI score set benchmark, our fine-tuned ranking model LambdaDockScore is better at identifying correct poses in its top-1 and top-5 predictions compared to EuDockScore, a state-of-the-art method. LambdaDockScore also improves upon baseline DFMDock ranking performance for scoring antibody-antigen complexes and protein-protein complexes with very large or small binding interfaces.

AI.tldr: Proposes LambdaDockScore, a protein-protein pose ranking model using the LambdaLoss loss from Learning-to-Rank, fine-tuned on top of DFMDock and outperforming EuDockScore on CAPRI benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Accurate scoring functions are essential for protein-protein interaction modeling to distinguish near-native poses from incorrect ones. Existing ranking methods can be improved by leveraging learning-to-rank techniques.
AI.method: A general framework applying the LambdaLoss loss function (Learning-to-Rank) to improve biomolecular interaction models. Tested by fine-tuning DFMDock's energy prediction head with LambdaLoss on an augmented dataset of 2.9M decoy poses derived from the DIPS dataset.
AI.result: On CAPRI score set targets, LambdaDockScore identifies correct poses better in top-1 and top-5 predictions than the state-of-the-art EuDockScore. It also improves on baseline DFMDock for antibody-antigen complexes and complexes with very large or small binding interfaces.
AI.conclusion: The LambdaLoss-based framework is general and effective for protein-protein pose ranking, yielding a model (LambdaDockScore) that surpasses state-of-the-art methods and improves baseline performance across challenging cases.

title: CANN: Commutative Algebra Neural Networks for Virus Classification
summary: The extensive diversity of viral genomes challenges alignment-free representations to capture both nucleotide composition and the higher-order organization of recurring sequence patterns. Conventional $k$-mer representations quantify pattern abundance but do not explicitly encode how these patterns are organized across scales. Here, we introduce CANN, an alignment-free framework that combines persistent commutative-algebraic descriptors with neural representation learning for viral family classification. CANN uses persistent facet descriptors to encode the multiscale organization of $k$-mer patterns and complementary $k$-mer counts to capture sequence composition. Convolutional and Transformer encoders independently learn latent representations of these features, and cosine distances within their respective embedding spaces are averaged before $k$-nearest-neighbor classification. Across multiple NCBI viral genome collections, CANN achieves robust family-level performance, with the fusion of encoder-specific distances consistently improving classification relative to either encoder alone. Evaluation on genomes present in the 2026 NCBI collection but absent from the 2024 reference set further supports generalization to unseen members of families already represented in the reference data. Together, these findings show that persistent commutative-algebraic descriptors can complement neural representations of viral genomes, linking algebraic descriptions of genomic organization with data-driven classification.

AI.tldr: CANN is an alignment-free framework for viral family classification that fuses persistent commutative-algebraic (facet) descriptors of multiscale k-mer organization with k-mer counts via convolutional and Transformer encoders, averaging cosine distances for k-NN classification.
AI.motivation: Viral genome diversity makes alignment-free representations hard: conventional k-mer representations capture composition/abundance but not the higher-order, multiscale organization of recurring sequence patterns.
AI.method: Persistent facet descriptors encode multiscale k-mer pattern organization; complementary k-mer counts capture composition. CNN and Transformer encoders learn separate latent representations, cosine distances in each embedding space are averaged, then k-NN classification.
AI.result: Across multiple NCBI viral genome collections, CANN achieves robust family-level performance; fusing encoder-specific distances consistently outperforms either encoder alone. Testing on genomes in the 2026 NCBI collection absent from the 2024 reference set shows generalization to unseen members of represented families.
AI.conclusion: Persistent commutative-algebraic descriptors complement neural representations of viral genomes, linking algebraic descriptions of genomic organization with data-driven classification.

title: Stochastic dynamics and synchronization in motif-based neuronal networks
summary: Neuronal networks exhibit complex dynamics shaped by connectivity and stochastic input. Empirical studies show that neuronal networks contain recurring subgraphs, or motifs, but the collective influence of different motif types after embedding in large stochastic networks remains less well understood. We construct a spiking network composed of six representative structural classes and examine how intrinsic noise, coupling strength, inter-motif connectivity, network size, and neuronal heterogeneity shape synchronization. Both motif- and network-level coherence peak at intermediate noise intensities, consistent with coherence resonance. Bidirectionally coupled pairs (M2) and the type-2 recurrent feed-forward loop (M3c) consistently exhibit high motif-level coherence. Rewiring these motifs while preserving local synapse number and strength produces some of the largest reductions in network coherence, showing that connection arrangement contributes beyond strong local coupling alone. M2 and M3c also exhibit frequent spike doublets, linking short inter-spike intervals with elevated coherence. Relative to a degree- and weight-matched random control, the motif-structured network reaches greater coherence at weaker noise. Increasing network size enhances coherence until the response begins to saturate, whereas applied-current heterogeneity lowers peak coherence and shifts the optimum toward stronger noise without erasing the relative differences among motif classes. These results show that local connection arrangement remains dynamically consequential after embedding and can shape noise-driven coherence at the population level.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how recurring network motifs shape synchronization in large stochastic spiking neuronal networks, showing motif arrangement remains dynamically consequential and can tune noise-driven coherence at the population level.
AI.motivation: Neuronal networks contain recurring subgraphs (motifs), but the collective influence of different motif types after embedding in large stochastic networks is not well understood.
AI.method: Constructed a spiking network of six representative structural motif classes and systematically varied intrinsic noise, coupling strength, inter-motif connectivity, network size, and neuronal heterogeneity to examine synchronization.
AI.result: Both motif- and network-level coherence peak at intermediate noise (coherence resonance). Bidirectionally coupled pairs (M2) and type-2 recurrent feed-forward loops (M3c) show high coherence and frequent spike doublets. Rewiring these motifs while preserving local synapse number and strength causes large coherence reductions. The motif-structured network outperforms degree- and weight-matched random controls at weaker noise, and coherence rises with network size until saturation.
AI.conclusion: Local connection arrangement remains dynamically consequential after embedding and can shape noise-driven coherence at the population level.

title: Stochastic Dynamics of Large-Scale Motif-Embedded Spiking Neuronal Networks
summary: We examine how local motif structure and global network topology jointly shape spiking dynamics in stochastic neuronal networks. Using networks of Izhikevich neurons with Erdős-Rényi (ER) and scale-free (SF) background connectivity, we compare motif-embedded networks with synapse-count-matched, non-motif controls under noise- and stimulus-driven protocols. Motif embedding increases noise-induced coherence in both topologies and provides a smaller improvement in signal transmission, while SF-based networks attain greater absolute coherence and transmit signals faster and more reliably than ER-based networks. Motif-rewiring experiments show that this benefit depends on the specific arrangement of intra-motif connections rather than on strong local connectivity alone: randomizing the motif skeleton reduces coherence overall, although rewiring the non-recurrent feed-forward loop and bi-parallel motif can increase it. Targeted ablation shows that the SF advantage depends in part on hub integrity; removing high-degree excitatory neurons impairs coherence and signal transmission more than matched random node or edge removal. Together, these results indicate that local motifs and global hubs make distinct, complementary contributions to coherent spiking dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how local network motifs and global topology (ER vs. scale-free) jointly shape coherent spiking dynamics, showing that motifs and hubs contribute distinct, complementary effects.
AI.motivation: Understanding how network structure at both local (motif) and global (topology) scales shapes spiking dynamics is important, yet their distinct and combined contributions remain unclear.
AI.method: Networks of Izhikevich neurons with Erdős-Rényi and scale-free connectivity were compared. Motif-embedded networks were tested against synapse-count-matched non-motif controls under noise- and stimulus-driven protocols, with motif-rewiring and targeted ablation experiments.
AI.result: Motif embedding increased noise-induced coherence in both topologies and gave smaller gains in signal transmission. SF networks showed greater absolute coherence and faster, more reliable transmission than ER networks. The benefit depended on specific intra-motif arrangement, not just strong local connectivity. Hub ablation impaired coherence and transmission more than matched random removal.
AI.conclusion: Local motifs and global hubs make distinct, complementary contributions to coherent spiking dynamics.

title: Synaptic placement reflects shared input in Drosophila descending neurons
summary: Network topology describes connections between neurons, whereas synaptic placement specifies how those connections are arranged within individual cells. How these levels of organization correspond remains incompletely understood. Here we show that connectivity between presynaptic neurons is reflected in relative input placement within Drosophila descending neurons (DNs). Across thousands of one-way DN connections in the independently reconstructed MaleCNS and FlyWire brains, inputs from sources also contacting the partner DN lay on average 9.4 and 8.0 μm nearer that partner's inputs along the receiver's neurites than other non-DN inputs. The same ordering held when source-input positions were fixed and partners with and without recorded source input were compared after standardizing reference-set size. In BANC and MaleCNS, shared input and measured spatial overlap provided complementary predictive information about DN interconnection. Two interconnected DNs sharing an ascending source differed in their identified cord outputs. Together, these findings link a three-neuron topological relationship to relative input placement, revealing a correspondence between network connectivity and the internal spatial organization of a receiving neuron.

AI.tldr: Connectivity between presynaptic neurons is reflected in the relative placement of their inputs along a Drosophila descending neuron's neurites, linking network topology to intracellular spatial organization.
AI.motivation: Network topology (inter-neuron connections) and synaptic placement (how connections are arranged within cells) are studied separately, and how these organizational levels correspond remains poorly understood.
AI.method: Analyzed thousands of one-way connections onto Drosophila descending neurons (DNs) in independently reconstructed MaleCNS and FlyWire brains, measuring distance between inputs from sources that also contact the partner DN versus other non-DN inputs; used standardized reference-set comparisons, plus BANC and MaleCNS data on shared input and spatial overlap.
AI.result: Inputs from sources that also contact the partner DN lay on average 9.4 μm (MaleCNS) and 8.0 μm (FlyWire) nearer that partner's inputs than other non-DN inputs. The ordering held when source-input positions were fixed. Shared input and spatial overlap gave complementary predictive information about DN interconnection. Two interconnected DNs sharing an ascending source differed in their identified cord outputs.
AI.conclusion: A three-neuron topological relationship maps onto relative input placement, revealing correspondence between network connectivity and the internal spatial organization of the receiving neuron.

title: StabilityArc: Decoding Protein Sequence Embeddings into Generalizable Stability Landscapes
comment: Accepted to Representations for the Physical Sciences Workshop @ NeurIPS 2026; 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables
summary: Every protein has a unique stability landscape, but the physical consequences of mutation are governed by recurring biochemical constraints. We test whether a shared decoder, trained on measurements from diverse proteins, can interpret these constraints in an unseen target, enabling cross-protein transfer for initial experimental round prescreening. We present StabilityArc , which maps frozen ESMC-600M residue representations through a shared RoPE transformer to an Lx20 matrix of substitution effects; a symmetric, contact-aware residual aids in predicting epistasis in simultaneous substitutions. In 66 strict leave-one-protein-out evaluations covering 134,794 ProteinGym variants, StabilityArc achieves 0.7134 Spearman correlation, exceeding the strongest zero-shot baseline, ProSST-2048 (0.6526), by 0.0608. We further explore the utility of this method by providing the score as a prior for Kermut, achieving Spearman correlation of 0.8280 across three supervised split schemes, improving on Kermut's reported 0.8167.

AI.tldr: StabilityArc is a shared decoder trained across diverse proteins to predict mutation effects, achieving strong cross-protein transfer for prescreening experiments.
AI.motivation: While each protein has a unique stability landscape, mutation effects follow recurring biochemical constraints. The paper tests whether a shared decoder trained on diverse proteins can interpret these constraints in unseen target proteins, enabling cross-protein transfer for initial experimental round prescreening.
AI.method: StabilityArc maps frozen ESMC-600M residue representations through a shared RoPE transformer to an Lx20 matrix of substitution effects. A symmetric, contact-aware residual component helps predict epistasis in simultaneous (multi-site) substitutions.
AI.result: In 66 strict leave-one-protein-out evaluations covering 134,794 ProteinGym variants, StabilityArc reaches 0.7134 Spearman correlation, surpassing the strongest zero-shot baseline ProSST-2048 (0.6526) by 0.0608. Used as a prior for Kermut, it achieves 0.8280 Spearman across three supervised split schemes, improving on Kermut's reported 0.8167.
AI.conclusion: A shared decoder over frozen protein language model representations enables effective cross-protein transfer of mutation effect prediction, and the score is also useful as a prior to boost supervised epistasis models like Kermut.

title: MEG-Mamba: A Scalable State-Space Foundation Model for Magnetoencephalography
summary: Magnetoencephalography (MEG) is an imaging technique that offers a non-invasive, millisecond-resolution view of human brain activity. The increasing availability of MEG data presents an opportunity to take advantage of a recent advance in artificial intelligence, namely self-supervised foundation models. Existing foundation models for MEG (and electroencephalography) have been built on a transformer architecture. Here, we introduce MEG-Mamba: a generative foundation model for neural activity (source reconstructed, parcellated MEG) built on a Mamba architecture. MEG-Mamba is trained to predict the next token of a discretised MEG signal, conditioned on a brain region and recording session. MEG-Mamba surpasses the generative fidelity of a transformer-based alternative (MEG-GPT) while pre-training in less time (22 vs 400 GPU-hours) and modelling a longer context (4 vs 0.32 s). We evaluate MEG-Mamba by examining the spatio-spectral characteristics of the data it generates and by interpreting its learned embeddings. Furthermore, we demonstrate that lightweight stimulus conditioning (LoRA) can be used to generate realistic task-evoked responses that are not included in pre-training. Our results suggest that Mamba is a promising backbone for scaling neural foundation models.

AI.tldr: MEG-Mamba is a generative foundation model for parcellated MEG built on the Mamba architecture, outperforming a transformer-based MEG-GPT in fidelity, training time, and context length.
AI.motivation: MEG offers non-invasive, millisecond-resolution brain imaging, and growing data availability enables self-supervised foundation models. Existing MEG/EEG foundation models rely on transformers; exploring alternative backbones could improve scaling.
AI.method: Train MEG-Mamba to predict the next token of discretised MEG signal, conditioned on brain region and recording session, using a Mamba architecture. Evaluate spatio-spectral characteristics and embeddings, and apply LoRA stimulus conditioning for task-evoked responses.
AI.result: MEG-Mamba exceeds MEG-GPT in generative fidelity while pre-training in 22 vs 400 GPU-hours and modeling 4 vs 0.32 s context. LoRA conditioning generates realistic task-evoked responses absent from pre-training.
AI.conclusion: Mamba is a promising backbone for scaling neural foundation models.

title: A multi-scale immuno-epidemiological behavioral model for influenza-like illness: connecting scales through symptom scores
summary: For many infectious diseases, behavior change is not a population-level reaction to rising case counts, but a personal one, triggered by how sick an individual feels. Yet most models fail to capture how illness severity drives this response. Multi-scale models that link the immunological scale to the epidemiological scale seem well-suited for capturing this behavior. Most multi-scale models link within-host viral load to population-level transmission rates through linking functions that are a function of viral load. However, viral load is often misaligned with symptom severity and thus possibly ill-suited for the purpose of informing behavior at a population level. We present a novel multi-scale model in which symptomatic individuals dynamically modify their transmission based on systemic symptom scores (a composite measure of muscle ache, fatigue, headache, and feverishness informed by within-host immune dynamics) while asymptomatic individuals do not change behavior. We find that stronger illness-driven behavior change delays and lowers the epidemic peak. Moreover, the resulting epidemic trajectory remains qualitatively similar to that of a standard SEIR model without behavior change, across several distinct choices of linking functions connecting the two scales. This stands in contrast to models where behavior change is driven by population-level feedback (e.g., reported cases or deaths), which can produce qualitatively distinct signatures such as plateaus, shoulders, or an elongated epidemic decline. In the case when an exponential function of symptom score is used as a linking function, we show that the standard SEIR model can closely reproduce the total number of infectious individuals at a given point in time generated through the multi-scale level.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a multi-scale model where symptomatic individuals change transmission based on within-host symptom scores, finding that illness-driven behavior change delays/lowers the epidemic peak but preserves SEIR-like dynamics.
AI.motivation: Behavior change in infectious diseases is often a personal reaction driven by how sick an individual feels, not a population-level response to case counts. Most models fail to capture how illness severity drives this response, and linking behavior to viral load is problematic since viral load is misaligned with symptom severity.
AI.method: The authors develop a multi-scale model linking within-host immune dynamics to population-level transmission. Symptomatic individuals dynamically modify their transmission based on systemic symptom scores (composite of muscle ache, fatigue, headache, feverishness), while asymptomatic individuals do not change behavior. They test several linking functions connecting the two scales.
AI.result: Stronger illness-driven behavior change delays and lowers the epidemic peak. The epidemic trajectory remains qualitatively similar to a standard SEIR model without behavior change across distinct linking functions. This contrasts with population-level feedback models (e.g., reported cases/deaths), which can produce qualitatively distinct signatures like plateaus, shoulders, or elongated declines. With an exponential symptom-score linking function, the standard SEIR model closely reproduces the total number of infectious individuals at a given time.
AI.conclusion: Illness-driven (symptom-score-based) behavior change produces epidemics that are qualitatively SEIR-like, unlike population-feedback-driven behavior change. This suggests symptom-based multi-scale models may be well-approximated by simpler SEIR models in certain cases.

title: One Inference, Four Failure Modes: Formal Models of Why Pain Location Fails
comment: This paper was previously the mathematical appendix of arXiv:2607.26297 and is developed here as a standalone treatment, with an introduction, a discussion of what would falsify each result, and its own glossary. arXiv:2607.26297v2 has been revised to remove that material; the two papers are companions and neither supersedes the other. 57 pages, 15 figures
summary:
Patient-reported pain location is diagnostically decisive for some presentations and nearly uninformative for others. A companion paper argues this is not one gradient of diagnostic utility but three distinct failures of localization. This paper gives those failures their mathematics and shows they are one object: a single Bayesian generative model failing at different nodes - the likelihood, the model class, and group- or context-dependence in that same likelihood. The count is not in dispute: the first three are failures of the inference that produces a felt location, and the fourth, added here, is a failure of reporting it.
  Anatomical multiplexing is a non-identifiable inverse problem: a rank-deficient referral matrix sends distinct causes to one report. Delocalized amplification is a change of generative model whose dynamics are a neural-field bifurcation, with spatial extent as the order parameter. Referred and atypical displacement is group- or context-dependence in the presentation likelihood - a probability, not a loss - whose consequence sits one layer downstream, in a decision threshold varying with group prevalence and cost. Repeated observation cannot reduce recoverable information about a fixed inferential target, an exact chain-rule identity, while practical value can fall.
  The fourth node is the report itself. A spatial Bayesian model factorizes mislocalization into referral blur, an anatomical offset and a precision-weighted cognitive override, and reproduces phantom-limb, mirror-box and central-post-stroke reports as regimes of one equation. It is estimable under conditions the paper states as necessary or sufficient rather than assuming them; Sec. 8 gives the design that meets them. One control is reported against the paper's own interest: the transport statistic first used to measure migration scores a stationary, spreading profile as though it had travelled.

AI.tldr: Pain localisation failures are reframed as a single Bayesian generative model failing at distinct nodes: likelihood, model class, group/context-dependence, and reporting. Each failure is given a mathematical formulation (rank-deficient inverse problem, neural-field bifurcation, decision-threshold shift, spatial Bayesian reporting model).
AI.motivation: Patient-reported pain location is diagnostically decisive for some conditions but nearly uninformative for others. A companion paper claims these are three distinct localisation failures rather than one utility gradient; this paper aims to formalise them mathematically and unify them as a single object.
AI.method: Formalises each failure mode: (1) anatomical multiplexing as a non-identifiable, rank-deficient inverse problem via a referral matrix; (2) delocalised amplification as a generative-model change with neural-field bifurcation dynamics, spatial extent as order parameter; (3) referred/atypical displacement as group/context-dependence in the presentation likelihood, affecting a downstream decision threshold. Adds a fourth node, the report, modelled with a spatial Bayesian factorisation into referral blur, anatomical offset, and precision-weighted cognitive override. States estimability conditions explicitly.
AI.result: The single model reproduces phantom-limb, mirror-box, and central-post-stroke reports as regimes of one equation. A chain-rule identity shows repeated observation cannot reduce recoverable information about a fixed inferential target, though practical value can fall. One control is reported against the paper's own interest: the transport statistic scores a stationary spreading profile as if it had travelled.
AI.conclusion: The three (plus one) localisation failures are unified as one Bayesian generative model failing at different nodes. The framework is estimable under stated necessary or sufficient conditions, with a design given in Sec. 8, and it self-reports a control result contrary to the authors' interest.

title: Molecular architecture of TE-seeded chromosome-naive initiation networks of protein-protein interactions delineates the Human Protein Map of the assembly of multiprotein complexes
summary: Upon binding to transposable elements seeded DNA, initiator transcription factors are poised to activate the hybrid assembly pathways (HAP) of endogenous multiprotein complexes (EMC) by iteratively engaging protein-protein interaction (PPI) cascade and creating cell type-specific pools of protein dimers. Here, molecular features and inferred biological functions of PPI cascade constituents were elucidated within the context of cell type-specific intracellular protein monomer pools documented in the Human Protein Atlas (HPA) of 154 human cell types. The following key features of the molecular architecture and functional performance of the 4 families of PPI cascade constituents were documented within the HPA contexts of intracellular proteomes: a) the ubiquitous expression and balanced representation; c) the universal availability and engagements; d) constitutive {invariant) and cell type-specific assembly profiles of EMCs. The biological relevance of the PPI cascades is demonstrated by cell-type-resolved multiprotein complex-engagement analysis across the HPA of human body, which faithfully recovers without supervision the intrinsic lineage structures of EMCs and lineage-specific master-regulator multiprotein assemblies. PPI cascade constituents have the capacity to generate 51,830 protein dimers within the proteome availability contexts of 154 types of human cells. Present analyses revealed critical impacts of the persistence of proteinopathy proteins that may cause the damage to the PPI cascade performance by sequestering 44 synaptic proteins. The sequestration of synaptic proteins withdraws structural-functional components of synapses suggesting a mechanism contributing to the pathogenesis of neurodegeneration. Conversely, reconstitution of availability of defined synaptic structural proteins appears to restore stoichiometry and recovers the lost assembly of synaptic protein dimers.

AI.tldr: This study characterizes the protein-protein interaction (PPI) cascade constituents underlying hybrid assembly pathways (HAP) of endogenous multiprotein complexes, analyzing their expression, availability, and assembly profiles across 154 human cell types using the Human Protein Atlas. Cell-type-resolved complex-engagement analysis recovers lineage structures unsupervised, reveals a capacity for 51,830 protein dimers, and shows how proteinopathy-driven sequestration of synaptic proteins disrupts assembly, offering a mechanism for neurodegeneration.
AI.motivation: Initiator transcription factors bound to transposable element-derived DNA activate hybrid assembly pathways of endogenous multiprotein complexes via iterative PPI cascades, generating cell type-specific protein dimer pools. The molecular features and biological functions of these PPI cascade constituents remained to be elucidated within cell type-specific proteome contexts.
AI.method: Analysis of PPI cascade constituents (4 families) within intracellular protein monomer pools documented in the Human Protein Atlas across 154 human cell types, performing cell-type-resolved multiprotein complex-engagement analysis.
AI.result: Key features of PPI cascade constituents were documented: ubiquitous expression and balanced representation, universal availability and engagement, and both constitutive and cell type-specific assembly profiles of EMCs. The analysis recovers intrinsic lineage structures and lineage-specific master-regulator assemblies without supervision. Constituents can generate 51,830 protein dimers across 154 cell types. Proteinopathy proteins impair PPI cascade performance by sequestering 44 synaptic proteins.
AI.conclusion: Sequestration of synaptic proteins withdraws structural-functional components of synapses, suggesting a mechanism in neurodegeneration pathogenesis. Conversely, reconstituting availability of defined synaptic structural proteins restores stoichiometry and recovers lost synaptic protein dimer assembly.

title: Multi-Scale Temporal Flows for Peptide Trajectory Generation
summary: Peptides occupy a particularly challenging regime of biomolecular dynamics. Short peptides lack a stable folded core and populate broad conformational ensembles, while cyclization adds ring closure, non-local residue coupling, and stereochemical diversity. Deep generative models have made remarkable progress in emulating molecular-dynamics trajectories directly, yet each is trained on windows cut at a fixed interval and therefore observes the process at a fixed temporal resolution. More fundamentally, none takes that interval as an input, so the physical time a window spans is never represented, leaving the sparse frames on which a peptide crosses between metastable states difficult to learn. Here, we introduce PepTIDE, a multi-scale temporal framework for peptide trajectory generation. The stride of each training window is drawn from a continuous range, so one model observes the same dynamics at many temporal resolutions, and an Adaptive Physical-Time Embedding encodes the relative interval of a window together with the absolute time of each frame, making the shared velocity field interval-aware. All frames are generated jointly through a stochastic-interpolant flow, and pair-aware invariant point attention captures the geometry and topology of both linear and cyclic peptides. On PepMD and a 50-system cyclic-peptide benchmark, PepTIDE reaches state-of-the-art distribution agreement and structural validity. Read in temporal order, its trajectories recover these sparse transition frames and reproduce inter-state fluxes more faithfully, confirming that modeling multiple temporal scales is what makes these rare events accessible.

AI.tldr: PepTIDE is a multi-scale temporal framework for generating peptide molecular-dynamics trajectories, where training windows use variable strides and an Adaptive Physical-Time Embedding encodes temporal intervals, achieving state-of-the-art distribution agreement and recovering rare transition events.
AI.motivation: Peptides are challenging for biomolecular dynamics: short peptides lack a stable folded core and populate broad ensembles, while cyclization adds ring closure, non-local coupling, and stereochemical diversity. Existing deep generative models for trajectories are trained on windows at a fixed interval, so they observe only one temporal resolution and never represent physical time span, making sparse frames where peptides cross metastable states hard to learn.
AI.method: PepTIDE draws each training window's stride from a continuous range so one model sees the same dynamics at many temporal resolutions. An Adaptive Physical-Time Embedding encodes both the relative interval of a window and the absolute time of each frame, making the shared velocity field interval-aware. All frames are generated jointly via a stochastic-interpolant flow, and pair-aware invariant point attention captures geometry/topology of both linear and cyclic peptides.
AI.result: On PepMD and a 50-system cyclic-peptide benchmark, PepTIDE achieves state-of-the-art distribution agreement and structural validity. When read in temporal order, its trajectories recover sparse transition frames and reproduce inter-state fluxes more faithfully.
AI.conclusion: Modeling multiple temporal scales is what makes rare transition events of peptides accessible, confirming the value of interval-aware, multi-scale trajectory generation.

title: Protocol for Discovering Convergent Molecular Networks across Multi-Omics Datasets Using Network Propagation
summary: Phenotypic outcomes arise from coordinated changes across molecular layers. Although multi-omics data capture complementary molecular signals, integrating them into coherent biological mechanisms remains challenging due to limited overlap at the gene level. Network propagation maps significant gene hits from each dataset onto a prior knowledge molecular interaction network and diffuses their signals to neighboring genes. Mathematical integration of propagated networks, followed by clustering and pathway enrichment, reveals shared molecular networks, pinpointing the core biology captured across orthogonal molecular layers.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a network propagation-based framework to integrate multi-omics data by diffusing gene-level signals over a prior molecular interaction network, then mathematically combining propagated networks to cluster and enrich pathways for uncovering shared core biology.
AI.motivation: Phenotypic outcomes stem from coordinated changes across molecular layers. Multi-omics data provide complementary signals, but limited gene-level overlap makes it hard to integrate them into coherent biological mechanisms.
AI.method: Network propagation is used: significant gene hits from each omics dataset are mapped onto a prior knowledge molecular interaction network, and their signals are diffused to neighboring genes. The propagated networks are then mathematically integrated and subjected to clustering and pathway enrichment.
AI.result: The integration reveals shared molecular networks across datasets, pinpointing the core biology captured across orthogonal molecular layers.
AI.conclusion: Network propagation-based integration of multi-omics data effectively overcomes limited gene overlap, enabling identification of shared molecular mechanisms and core biology across complementary molecular layers.

title: A High-Density EEG Dataset for Stimulus-Driven Auditory Attention
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables.Dataset available at at https://zenodo.org/records/20557225. Code available at https://github.com/yanruofan628/saad-preprocessing
summary: Stimulus-driven auditory attention determines which sound gains priority when multiple sources compete without an explicit listening goal, yet most computational studies focus either on acoustic salience or on decoding predefined attended targets. This study investigates instruction-free auditory competition using the Stimulus-driven Auditory Attention (SAAD) paradigm and develops a neurophysiologically informed framework that integrates stimulus-derived sound priority with trial-specific EEG evidence. Behavioral analysis using a Bradley--Terry model showed that sound priority estimated from previous competitions generalized to unseen sound pairings, improving held-out prediction from an AUC of 0.577 to 0.718. EEG analysis further revealed mid-to-late centro-temporal lateralization associated with the reported selection side, with neural information remaining predictive beyond acoustic asymmetry. Guided by these findings, the proposed model first estimates a latent priority for each competing sound and forms relative stimulus evidence from their difference. A multi-scale EEG pathway with complementary signed and power-based readouts then extracts trial-specific neural evidence, which is incorporated through gated decision-level integration. The framework is evaluated using mirror-constrained and pairing-held-out protocols, together with representative acoustic, EEG, multimodal baselines, and systematic ablations. The results support a computational account in which spontaneous auditory selection reflects the interaction between generalizable stimulus priority and trial-specific neural variability.

AI.tldr: The paper studies instruction-free auditory attention competition using the SAAD paradigm and proposes a neurophysiologically informed framework combining generalizable stimulus-driven sound priority with trial-specific EEG evidence.
AI.motivation: Most computational studies focus either on acoustic salience or decoding predefined attended targets, leaving stimulus-driven (instruction-free) auditory competition underexplored.
AI.method: Using the Stimulus-driven Auditory Attention paradigm, behavioral analysis via a Bradley--Terry model; EEG analysis of centro-temporal lateralization; a model that estimates latent priority per sound, forms relative stimulus evidence from their difference, and uses a multi-scale EEG pathway with signed and power-based readouts integrated via gated decision-level fusion. Evaluated with mirror-constrained and pairing-held-out protocols against acoustic, EEG, and multimodal baselines plus ablations.
AI.result: Sound priority generalized to unseen pairings, improving held-out AUC from 0.577 to 0.718. EEG showed mid-to-late centro-temporal lateralization tied to reported selection side, with neural information predictive beyond acoustic asymmetry.
AI.conclusion: Spontaneous auditory selection reflects the interaction between generalizable stimulus priority and trial-specific neural variability.

title: Fold'EM: Direct atomic structure inference from Cryo-EM particles
summary: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) has become a widely adopted technique for biomolecular structure determination. The conventional cryo-EM computational pipeline first combines many particle images to reconstruct an electrostatic potential (ESP) map and then fits an atomic model to the recovered map. Density reconstruction has high sample complexity, requiring large numbers of particle images and making structure determination high-cost and low-throughput, particularly for heterogeneous samples. Downstream atomic model building, in turn, becomes increasingly difficult as the resolution of the reconstructed map deteriorates. Protein structure prediction models provide strong sequence-derived priors on atomic structure, and experiment-guided approaches can use these priors to recover structures consistent with experimental measurements. Yet, in cryo-EM, such priors are typically integrated only after density reconstruction during atomic model fitting. We introduce Fold'EM, an inference-time framework that combines priors from protein generative models directly with cryo-EM particle images to determine atomic models from a small number of single particle images, bypassing both intermediate density reconstruction and downstream model building against the reconstructed map. Across synthetic and experimental cryo-EM datasets, Fold'EM recovers accurate atomic structures both with known particle orientations and in an ab-initio setting where orientations are inferred jointly with structure. In heterogeneous datasets, Fold'EM further resolves distinct conformational states from mixed particle populations without separately reconstructing a density map and building an atomic model for each state. We believe these results open new avenues for structure determination in the low-sample regime and for characterizing low-population conformational states directly from cryo-EM particles.

AI.tldr: Fold'EM is an inference-time framework that combines protein generative model priors directly with cryo-EM particle images to determine atomic structures from few particles, bypassing density reconstruction and downstream model building.
AI.motivation: Conventional cryo-EM pipelines reconstruct a density map from many particles then fit an atomic model, requiring large sample sizes and suffering at low resolution. Existing structure-prediction priors are typically only integrated after density reconstruction, leaving the low-sample regime unaddressed.
AI.method: Fold'EM integrates protein generative-model priors directly with cryo-EM particle images at inference time. It determines atomic models without intermediate density reconstruction or downstream model fitting, operating both with known particle orientations and in an ab-initio setting where orientations are jointly inferred with structure.
AI.result: Across synthetic and experimental cryo-EM datasets, Fold'EM recovers accurate atomic structures from a small number of particles. In heterogeneous datasets, it resolves distinct conformational states from mixed particle populations without separately reconstructing densities or building models per state.
AI.conclusion: The results open new avenues for structure determination in the low-sample regime and for characterizing low-population conformational states directly from cryo-EM particles.

title: CPathOGen: Spatially and Morphologically Controlled H&E Counterfactuals for Probing Pathology Models
summary: Computational pathology models infer biologically and clinically meaningful outcomes from histology, but their predictions are shaped by complex, intertwined tissue signals whose roles are important to understand. Common pixel- and feature-space perturbations can produce implausible tissue, making model responses difficult to interpret. We introduce CPathOGen, a conditional latent-diffusion framework for generating paired H\&E counterfactuals with explicit controls over cellular spatial organization, nuclear morphology, and stain appearance. Cellular maps condition spatial structure through a spatial encoder, while a morphology/appearance vector modulates denoising through blockwise feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM). On held-out H\&E tiles, CPathOGen generates visually plausible tissue with improved distributional agreement after spatially guided selection, as reflected by lower Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and Kernel Inception Distance (KID); generated cells track requested abundance and position, and measured morphology and color vary monotonically with their controls. We use these verified interventions to probe pathology encoders with endpoint heads, task-specific classifiers, and survival models. Responses are quantified using total variation distance and prediction-flip rate. We further introduce the Biology-Nuisance Sensitivity Ratio, a metric that contrasts model sensitivity to biologically motivated morphology and spatial factors with sensitivity to non-biological, stain-related nuisance variation. CPathOGen provides a practical, fidelity-audited framework for evaluating robustness and controlled feature sensitivity in computational pathology model. \href{https://github.com/a12dongithub/PathOGen}{GitHub} and \href{https://huggingface.co/a12donhf/CPathOGen}{Hugging~Face}.

AI.tldr: CPathOGen is a conditional latent-diffusion framework that generates paired H&E counterfactuals with explicit control over cellular spatial organization, nuclear morphology, and stain appearance, enabling fidelity-audited probing of computational pathology models.
AI.motivation: Computational pathology model predictions are shaped by intertwined tissue signals, but common pixel- and feature-space perturbations yield implausible tissue, making model responses hard to interpret.
AI.method: A spatial encoder conditions spatial structure from cellular maps, while a morphology/appearance vector modulates denoising via blockwise FiLM in a conditional latent-diffusion framework, generating paired counterfactuals with controlled attributes.
AI.result: Generated tissue is visually plausible with lower FID/KID after spatially guided selection; cells track requested abundance/position, and morphology and color vary monotonically with controls. Probing reveals responses via total variation distance and prediction-flip rate, plus a new Biology-Nuisance Sensitivity Ratio.
AI.conclusion: CPathOGen provides a practical, fidelity-audited framework for evaluating robustness and controlled feature sensitivity in computational pathology models.

title: Analysis of Quantized and Efficiently Adapted Protein Language Models
summary: Background: Protein language models (PLMs) are increasingly used for sequence generation and property prediction, but their size makes fine-tuning and deployment expensive. The effects of quantization and parameter efficient fine-tuning on performance, representations and generation remain insufficiently characterized. Results: We evaluated 4-bit quantization and low-rank adapter fine-tuning (QLoRA) across ESM-2, ESMC, ProtBERT, ProtT5, Ankh, Ankh3 and Profluent-E1. Across protein prediction tasks, many model-task pairs retained more than 90% of full fine-tuning performance. Peak GPU memory savings approached 90% for the largest models, although performance and efficiency varied by model, dataset and training configuration. QLoRA often preserved early-layer representations while inducing task-specific adaptations in middle and late layers, resembling full fine-tuning with smaller representational changes. Training speed and power effects were more varied. For unconditional generation with ProLLaMA, ProtGPT2, ProGen2, ProteinGLM and ESM3, 4-bit quantization largely preserved predicted structural and sequence-level properties, but token-level analysis revealed model-dependent shifts in autoregressive output distributions. Conclusion: QLoRA and 4-bit quantization reduce PLM computational requirements, particularly GPU memory usage. Our results support QLoRA as a first-pass strategy for memory limited adaptation, reserving full fine-tuning for challenging tasks, unstable architectures or low validation recovery. For generative PLMs, sequence-level and structural metrics should be complemented with distributional analysis, since downstream predictions alone may miss quantization-induced shifts. These approaches can broaden access to large-scale protein modelling while requiring model- and task-specific validation.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates 4-bit quantization and QLoRA (low-rank adapter fine-tuning) across seven protein language models. QLoRA retains >90% of full fine-tuning performance on many tasks and cuts peak GPU memory by up to ~90%, while preserving early-layer representations. For generative PLMs, 4-bit quantization largely preserves structural/sequence properties but introduces model-dependent shifts in token-level distributions.
AI.motivation: Protein language models (PLMs) achieve strong performance in sequence generation and property prediction, but their large size makes fine-tuning and deployment computationally expensive. The effects of quantization and parameter-efficient fine-tuning on performance, representations, and generation remain insufficiently characterized.
AI.method: The authors applied 4-bit quantization and low-rank adapter fine-tuning (QLoRA) and compared them against full fine-tuning across a range of PLMs: ESM-2, ESMC, ProtBERT, ProtT5, Ankh, Ankh3, and Profluent-E1 for prediction tasks, and ProLLaMA, ProtGPT2, ProGen2, ProteinGLM, and ESM3 for unconditional generation. They assessed task performance, GPU memory/speed/power efficiency, layer-wise representational changes, and token-level output distributions.
AI.result: Many model-task pairs retained over 90% of full fine-tuning performance. Peak GPU memory savings approached ~90% for the largest models, though performance and efficiency varied by model, dataset, and training configuration. QLoRA often preserved early-layer representations while inducing task-specific adaptations in middle and late layers. Training speed and power effects were more varied. For generation, 4-bit quantization largely preserved predicted structural and sequence-level properties, but token-level analysis revealed model-dependent shifts in autoregressive output distributions.
AI.conclusion: QLoRA and 4-bit quantization substantially reduce PLM computational requirements, especially GPU memory, supporting QLoRA as a first-pass strategy for memory-limited adaptation while reserving full fine-tuning for challenging tasks, unstable architectures, or low validation recovery. For generative PLMs, sequence-level and structural metrics should be complemented by distributional analysis, since downstream predictions alone may miss quantization-induced shifts. These approaches broaden access to large-scale protein modeling but require model- and task-specific validation.

title: ORBIT-FMIB: Tracking Order-Resolved Epistatic Information Through ESM-2
summary:
Protein foundation models support mutation-effect and structural prediction, but predictive performance alone does not reveal which forms of biological interaction information remain accessible through model depth. We ask whether ESM-2 retains higher-order epistatic information as strongly as first- and second-order information across its representation hierarchy, introducing ORBIT-FMIB, a diagnostic framework combining Walsh-based interaction decomposition with subset-conditioned neural dependence estimation. The method is validated on synthetic landscapes with known interaction structure before being applied to the dense four-site GB1 fitness landscape using frozen ESM-2 representations.
  An initial production run suggested ESM-2 retains higher-order epistatic information less well than lower-order information ($Δ_{\mathrm{HO-LO}}=-0.107$). An independent replication of the complete measurement grid, under matched GPU hardware and identical critic seeds, substantially reduced this contrast ($Δ_{\mathrm{HO-LO}}=-0.017$), and its sign was unstable across otherwise-defensible evaluation-pairing choices applied to the same trained critics ($-0.011$ to $+0.015$). We therefore do not currently have robust evidence that ESM-2 selectively loses higher-order epistatic information, nor that retention is equal across orders; the directional question remains open. The measurement protocol itself, including its documented removal of a positional-subset shortcut in pooled critics, remains validated and is unaffected by this finding. ORBIT-FMIB is offered as a diagnostic framework for probing interaction structure in protein foundation models; this study's own replication result illustrates why such probing requires adequately-powered reproducibility checks before its output is treated as a biological finding.

AI.tldr: ORBIT-FMIB probes whether ESM-2 retains higher-order epistatic information across its representation hierarchy using Walsh-based interaction decomposition; a replication rendered the initial contrast statistically fragile and the directional question open.
AI.motivation: Protein foundation models (e.g., ESM-2) are used for mutation-effect and structural prediction, but predictive performance does not reveal what forms of biological interaction information (first-, second-, higher-order epistasis) remain accessible through model depth. The paper asks whether ESM-2 selectively loses higher-order epistatic information.
AI.method: ORBIT-FMIB, a diagnostic framework combining Walsh-based interaction decomposition with subset-conditioned neural dependence estimation. Validated on synthetic landscapes with known interaction structure, then applied to the dense four-site GB1 fitness landscape using frozen ESM-2 representations. Includes an independent replication of the full measurement grid under matched GPU hardware and identical critic seeds, plus sensitivity to evaluation-pairing choices.
AI.result: Initial run showed lower retention of higher-order vs lower-order information (Δ_HO-LO = -0.107). Independent replication reduced the contrast to -0.017, with unstable sign across defensible evaluation-pairing choices (-0.011 to +0.015). No robust evidence of selective loss or equal retention across orders.
AI.conclusion: The directional question about ESM-2's order-dependent epistatic retention remains open. The measurement protocol (including removal of a positional-subset shortcut in pooled critics) stays validated. ORBIT-FMIB is a useful diagnostic, but such probing requires adequately powered reproducibility checks before outputs are treated as biological findings.

title: Neuromorphic Pseudo-Random Number Generators with a Low Power Hardware Implementation
summary: Pseudo-random number generation often requires trade-offs among quality, power consumption, and bandwidth to produce unpredictable sequences of numbers. The brain, on the other hand, efficiently generates unpredictable output complex network dynamics occurring in a high-dimensional state. This state, which is hypothesized to be chaotic, relies on the balance between excitation and inhibition. Here, we investigated if computational models of these chaotic balanced states can be harnessed for Neuromorphic Pseudo-Random Number Generators (NPRNGs) in low power hardware. We successfully constructed a balanced spiking neural network model consisting of leaky-integrate-and-fire neurons that could be readily implemented in low power FPGAs and used as a NPRNG. The prototyped NPRNG consumed 3.24 mW during operation and produced pseudo-random numbers at 120kbps. In both hardware and software instantiations, NPRNGs produce high-quality random numbers as validated by standard metrics for testing RNG quality.

AI.tldr: A balanced spiking neural network of leaky-integrate-and-fire neurons is built and deployed on low-power FPGAs as a neuromorphic pseudo-random number generator (NPRNG), consuming 3.24 mW at 120 kbps while producing high-quality random numbers.
AI.motivation: Pseudo-random number generation typically demands trade-offs among quality, power consumption, and bandwidth. The brain, however, efficiently generates unpredictable output via complex high-dimensional chaotic network dynamics relying on an excitation-inhibition balance, suggesting a bio-inspired alternative for low-power hardware.
AI.method: The authors built a balanced spiking neural network model composed of leaky-integrate-and-fire neurons, exploiting chaotic balanced-state dynamics. The model was designed for ready implementation on low-power FPGAs and instantiated as an NPRNG in both hardware and software.
AI.result: The prototyped NPRNG consumed 3.24 mW during operation and produced pseudo-random numbers at 120 kbps. In both hardware and software instantiations, the NPRNG generated high-quality random numbers, validated by standard metrics for testing RNG quality.
AI.conclusion: Computational models of chaotic balanced brain states can be effectively harnessed for neuromorphic pseudo-random number generation, achieving low power consumption and high-quality randomness suitable for low-power hardware.

title: Increasing Width Allows Greedy Layer-wise Training to Rival End-to-End Backpropagation in Self-Supervised Learning
summary: End-to-end backpropagation has been the dominant mode of training in deep learning, allowing for the coordination of parameter updates across layers of a neural network. Prior studies have explored alternative -- and, in some cases, simpler -- training mechanisms, showing that they can sometimes achieve performance similar to backpropagation. However, the architectural conditions under which locally optimized networks, which avoid end-to-end backpropagation of error, can learn representations comparable to those learned through end-to-end training remain unclear. We aim to answer this question in the context of self-supervised learning, an important framework for large-scale pretraining in artificial intelligence. Here, we investigate how network width and depth affect the efficacy of greedy layer-wise and end-to-end self-supervised training in convolutional networks. We find that in wider networks, the benefits of end-to-end backpropagation over greedy layer-wise training shrink: in relatively shallow and very wide networks, we even observed higher performance in models trained with greedy layer-wise training. Subsequent analysis of the representations formed by these networks shows that very wide greedy-trained networks exhibit more favorable representational geometry than do networks trained end-to-end with backpropagation. This work shows that width can compensate for restricted credit assignment and identifies differences in representational geometry as a potential mechanism for their improved performance.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how network width and depth affect greedy layer-wise vs. end-to-end self-supervised training in CNNs, finding that width can compensate for restricted credit assignment.
AI.motivation: End-to-end backpropagation dominates deep learning training, but alternative local training mechanisms sometimes achieve similar performance. Yet it remains unclear under what architectural conditions locally optimized networks can learn representations comparable to end-to-end training, especially in self-supervised learning.
AI.method: The authors investigate how network width and depth influence the efficacy of greedy layer-wise versus end-to-end self-supervised training in convolutional networks, then analyze the representational geometry of the resulting networks.
AI.result: In wider networks, the advantage of end-to-end backpropagation over greedy layer-wise training shrinks. In relatively shallow and very wide networks, greedy layer-wise training even achieved higher performance. Very wide greedy-trained networks showed more favorable representational geometry than end-to-end trained ones.
AI.conclusion: Network width can compensate for restricted credit assignment, and differences in representational geometry are identified as a potential mechanism for the improved performance of greedy layer-wise training.

title: MorphoBranch: A Fine-Structure-Preserving Workbench for Morphometric Analysis of Branched Cellular Structures
summary: Background and Objectives: Fluorescence-labeled cellular arbors provide readouts of neuronal and microglial morphology, but fine and weakly labeled processes are prone to fragmentation and false connections that bias skeleton-based measurements. We present MorphoBranch, a fine-structure-preserving, human-reviewable workbench for morphometry of branched cellular structures. Methods: MorphoBranch combines a deterministic Morphometry Engine with an LLM-assisted Refinement Engine. The Mor- phometry Engine implements an image-to-graph workflow integrating multiscale structural evidence extraction, hysteresis segmen- tation, evidence-constrained skeleton refinement, and graph-based morphometry. The Refinement Engine maps natural-language requests to registered actions for parameter adjustment, preview execution, metric reporting, and unsupported-request handling, while image processing and quantitative computation remain deterministic and reviewable. Results: MorphoBranch was evaluated on two public neuronal axon datasets, AxonMIP and AxonStack, and the in-house Cell- Morph dataset of microglial fluorescence images. It achieved the highest Skeleton F1 and clDice and the lowest length-estimation error among the evaluated methods on all three datasets, while also achieving the highest Dice and IoU on AxonMIP and Axon- Stack. Across 150 natural-language tasks, the Refinement Engine achieved a 94.0% end-to-end success rate. Conclusions: These results demonstrate that MorphoBranch provides a reproducible, human-reviewable workflow for mor- phometric analysis of branched cellular structures. It supports fine-structure-preserving quantification across neuronal axon and microglial fluorescence images while maintaining inspectable and reproducible analysis workflows.

AI.tldr: MorphoBranch is a human-reviewable workbench combining a deterministic Morphometry Engine with an LLM-assisted Refinement Engine for fine-structure-preserving morphometry of branched cellular structures, outperforming baselines on neuronal axon and microglial datasets.
AI.motivation: Fluorescence-labeled cellular arbors provide readouts of neuronal and microglial morphology, but fine and weakly labeled processes are prone to fragmentation and false connections that bias skeleton-based measurements.
AI.method: Combines a deterministic Morphometry Engine (multiscale structural evidence extraction, hysteresis segmentation, evidence-constrained skeleton refinement, graph-based morphometry) with an LLM-assisted Refinement Engine that maps natural-language requests to registered actions (parameter adjustment, preview, metric reporting, unsupported-request handling), while image processing and computation remain deterministic and reviewable.
AI.result: Evaluated on AxonMIP, AxonStack, and in-house CellMorph microglia datasets: achieved highest Skeleton F1, clDice, and lowest length-estimation error on all three; highest Dice and IoU on AxonMIP and AxonStack. Refinement Engine reached 94.0% end-to-end success across 150 natural-language tasks.
AI.conclusion: MorphoBranch provides a reproducible, human-reviewable workflow for morphometric analysis of branched cellular structures, enabling fine-structure-preserving quantification across neuronal axon and microglial fluorescence images with inspectable, reproducible workflows.

title: Efficient Convex Optimization Methods for State-Space Heartbeat Dynamics Models with Gamma Generalized Linear Models
summary: Objective: This work proposes a dynamic state-space statistical model of heartbeat dynamics whose optimal state estimate can be solved efficiently with convex optimization and used to assess autonomic and cardiovascular health. Methods: This state-space model combines a Gauss-Markov process prior with gamma emissions using a log-link function. Parameters are estimated using a static version of the model, and alternating direction method of multipliers is used to efficiently find the optimal maximum a priori latent state estimate. Model selection is performed by finding the tradeoff between model size and model fit using the partial autocorrelation function. Results: We demonstrate in synthetically generated heartbeats that this model is able to closely recover the underlying latent weights. Then, we show using a tilt table dataset that this statistical model is able to better capture sharp transients in heart rate patterns than traditional local averaging methods. In addition, combining heart beat timings with information from other organs such as the respiratory phase, we show that our statistical modeling framework enables the extraction of information-theoretic measures to quantify inter-organ coupling such as respiratory sinus arrythmia. Conclusion: This statistical framework for modeling heartbeat dynamics provides an efficient framework that can provide physiologically meaningful insights. Significance: This work broadens potential tools that can be used to assess heartbeat dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dynamic state-space model of heartbeat dynamics, solvable via convex optimization, to assess autonomic and cardiovascular health.
AI.motivation: Traditional local averaging methods poorly capture sharp transients in heart rate patterns and lack a principled framework for quantifying inter-organ coupling, motivating a more effective statistical model of heartbeat dynamics.
AI.method: A state-space model combining a Gauss-Markov process prior with gamma emissions via a log-link function. Parameters are estimated in a static version; the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) finds the optimal maximum a priori latent state estimate; model selection balances size vs. fit using the partial autocorrelation function.
AI.result: On synthetic heartbeats, the model closely recovers underlying latent weights. On a tilt table dataset, it captures sharp heart rate transients better than local averaging. Combined with respiratory phase, it enables information-theoretic measures of inter-organ coupling such as respiratory sinus arrhythmia.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers an efficient, physiologically meaningful tool for modeling heartbeat dynamics, broadening the tools available to assess heartbeat dynamics.

title: Auditable Algebraic Counting Field for Cryptic-Pocket Detection from Apo Structures
comment: Accepted for publication in Pacific Symposium on Biocomputing (PSB) 2027
summary: Cryptic ligand-binding pockets are not apparent in experimentally determined apo structures, making them difficult to identify from unbound receptor geometry. A complementary challenge is to make the structural measurements and learned evidence behind each prediction directly inspectable. We introduce a supervised algebraic counting field (ACF) for predicting cryptic-pocket residues from apo structures. ACF compiles explicit geometric, physicochemical, and topological features into compact, integer-weighted lookup tables. Each prediction score can be reconstructed from feature values, training counts, table weights, and spatial aggregation, without sequence search, structural-template transfer, or a protein language model at inference. We evaluate ACF on CryptoBench and two locked external collections, separating ranking performance from the effects of residue-calling budgets. On an external set of 57 post-CryptoBench apo-holo units, ACF exceeded P2Rank by +0.044 in mean paired ROC-AUC (multiplicity-adjusted 95% CI [+0.010, +0.079]). The advantage was dataset-dependent: official-fold ROC-AUC and matched-budget F1 differences against P2Rank remained unresolved, and a second external evaluation did not confirm gains from added structural features. ACF thus provides a compact predictor with externally validated signal and an inspectable path from structural measurements and training counts to residue scores.

AI.tldr: ACF is a supervised algebraic counting field that predicts cryptic-pocket residues from apo structures using interpretable integer-weighted lookup tables, showing external signal but dataset-dependent gains over P2Rank.
AI.motivation: Cryptic ligand-binding pockets are invisible in apo structures, making them hard to detect from unbound geometry. Additionally, most existing predictors are opaque, so the structural evidence behind each prediction cannot be directly inspected.
AI.method: ACF compiles explicit geometric, physicochemical, and topological features into compact integer-weighted lookup tables. Each prediction score is reconstructable from feature values, training counts, table weights, and spatial aggregation, without sequence search, template transfer, or a protein language model at inference.
AI.result: Evaluated on CryptoBench and two locked external collections. On 57 post-CryptoBench apo-holo units, ACF beat P2Rank by +0.044 mean paired ROC-AUC (95% CI [+0.010, +0.079]). However, official-fold ROC-AUC and matched-budget F1 differences were unresolved, and a second external evaluation did not confirm gains from added structural features.
AI.conclusion: ACF offers a compact, externally validated cryptic-pocket predictor with an inspectable path from structural measurements and training counts to residue scores, though its advantage over P2Rank is dataset-dependent.

title: Selection rules for the harmonic spectroscopy of animal decisions
summary: Spectroscopy reads structure by sending a structured probe into a system and measuring what comes back. Here we apply this principle to animal decision-making. Harmonic Theory casts choice as motion on an angular landscape over heading, whose Fourier components form an animal's decision spectrum. We show that the arrangement of cues enters that landscape as a structure factor, so it factors like a diffraction amplitude, and symmetry imposes selection rules: a p-fold cue array annihilates every harmonic that is not a multiple of p, and sweeping two cues apart draws a notch through each harmonic. Cue geometry becomes a tunable probe: the experimenter sets which harmonics an experiment can see. We read these spectra from public recordings of flies, schooling fish, larval zebrafish, mice and a swimming alga, and from the fly's neural compass, where symmetric scenes suppress the forbidden harmonics and breaking that symmetry restores them. Measuring the compass form factor favours the theory's smooth bump over its square one, and raising cue contrast narrows that bump in every fly. A width fitted to one harmonic then predicts the next. Cue geometry is a spectrometer for decisions, and symmetry sets what it can see.

AI.tldr: Harmonic Theory treats animal choice as motion on an angular "decision landscape" over heading, whose Fourier components form a decision spectrum. Cue arrangement acts as a structure factor with selection rules, letting experimenters use cue geometry as a tunable spectrometer to probe decision-making, validated across flies, fish, zebrafish, mice, algae, and the fly neural compass.
AI.motivation: Spectroscopy reads structure by probing a system and measuring the response; the paper applies this analogy to animal decision-making, aiming to explain how cue arrangement shapes decisions and to provide a principled framework for probing the underlying neural/behavioral landscape.
AI.method: Cast choice as motion on an angular landscape over heading, with Fourier components forming a decision spectrum. Cues enter the landscape as a structure factor behaving like a diffraction amplitude, imposing symmetry selection rules (p-fold cue array annihilates non-multiple-of-p harmonics; sweeping cues apart creates a notch in each harmonic). Spectra are read from public recordings (flies, schooling fish, larval zebrafish, mice, swimming alga) and the fly neural compass, plus compass form-factor and cue-contrast manipulations.
AI.result: Symmetry suppresses forbidden harmonics in the fly compass, and breaking symmetry restores them. Compass form factor favors the theory's smooth bump over a square bump; raising cue contrast narrows the bump consistently across flies. A width fitted to one harmonic successfully predicts the next harmonic.
AI.conclusion: Cue geometry functions as a spectrometer for decisions, with symmetry determining what harmonics can be observed, providing a unifying, testable account of animal decision-making.

title: Compartmental epidemiological models with infection-driven immune escape
summary: We propose and study a compartmental epidemiological model that incorporates both waning immunity and mutation-driven immune escape into a single-strain framework. The model, termed SIRCm, extends the SIRC (Susceptible-Infected-Recovered-Cross-immune) model, in which recovered individuals pass through an intermediate cross-immune class before returning to full susceptibility. In SIRCm, both the rate of immune waning and the rate of immune escape are amplified by a feedback function tied to the current level of infection. We study two formulations of this feedback, a transmission-driven model, in which mutation opportunities arise at the point of new infection, and a prevalence-driven model, in which they arise in proportion to the infected population alone. For both models and any feedback strength, we prove existence of an endemic equilibrium using persistence theory, and characterize its behavior analytically in the weak and strong-feedback limits, recovering the SIRC and SIS models, respectively, as limiting cases. Unlike the SIRC model, we show that the SIRCm endemic equilibrium is unstable in certain parameter regimes. This leads to novel behavior, even in the absence of seasonal forcing.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SIRCm, a compartmental epidemiological model extending SIRC by adding waning immunity and mutation-driven immune escape, with feedback tied to infection levels, proving endemic equilibrium existence and showing novel instability.
AI.motivation: Existing models like SIRC capture waning immunity but not mutation-driven immune escape; integrating both, with feedback from infection levels, is needed to understand instability and novel dynamics without seasonal forcing.
AI.method: Extends the SIRC model into SIRCm, incorporating waning immunity and immune escape amplified by infection-level feedback. Two formulations are studied: transmission-driven (mutation at new infection) and prevalence-driven (mutation proportional to infected population). Use persistence theory and analytic limits (weak/strong feedback).
AI.result: Endemic equilibrium existence proven for both models at any feedback strength. Weak feedback recovers SIRC; strong feedback recovers SIS. The SIRCm endemic equilibrium is unstable in certain parameter regimes, yielding novel behavior even without seasonal forcing.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating mutation-driven immune escape with infection feedback produces instability and richer dynamics than SIRC, highlighting the importance of immune escape mechanisms in epidemiological modeling.

title: Can LLMs Reliably Annotate Bioassay Metadata to Improve Data Readiness?
comment: Accepted to the AIDaR workshop at NeurIPS
summary: The emergence of foundation models for molecular property prediction requires a high degree of AI data readiness, including reliable metadata annotation. However, both public repositories and industrial screening databases suffer from missing, inconsistent, or conflated assay annotations. In this work, we quantify the extent of missing annotations in PubChem for the BioAssay Ontology (BAO) assay format and physical detection method fields and investigate whether open-source and proprietary large language models (LLMs) can reliably predict and audit metadata annotations directly from the assay text.
