In our assessment, we found that the annotation coverage across PubChem's $\sim$2 million bioassays is critically sparse, 36\% lacking an assay format, 89\% a BioAssay type, and >99.9\% any BAO-mapped assay format or detection technology term. This motivates the need for automated test-metadata curation. Using evaluation sets derived from PubChem and ChEMBL, we assess the agreement of seven open-source and proprietary LLMs with existing silver labels. Recall is at least 0.96 for biochemical and cell-based assay formats, with a similar pattern for detection technology, although disagreements increase on under-represented classes. Manual inspection shows that many of these disagreements trace back to inconsistencies between silver sources rather than to LLM error. Moreover, in a qualitative study with a senior industrial curator, LLM-generated evidence prompted the expert to revise some of their own labels, showing LLMs can flag potentially mislabeled assays. Across the study, performance differences between proprietary and open-source models were small. Together, these results suggest LLMs can support the large-scale annotation and auditing of assay metadata, though per-class reliability estimates and targeted human review remain necessary before such labels enter downstream ML pipelines.

AI.motivation: Foundation models for molecular property prediction require high AI data readiness, including reliable metadata annotation. However, public repositories and industrial screening databases suffer from missing, inconsistent, or conflated assay annotations, which undermines downstream ML pipelines.

title: Autocatalysis and Boundary Stability in Chemical Reaction Systems
summary: The next-generation matrix method is a powerful tool for computing the basic reproduction number in compartmental mathematical models of infectious diseases. The method has been recently extended to mathematical biochemistry, where it can be used to establish parameter regions of stability and instability for boundary steady states. Several significant challenges in its application remain, however, particularly around establishing conditions under which the method is mathematically valid, computationally tractable, and biologically meaningful in the biochemical setting. In this paper, we address these challenges by shifting the interpretation from new infections in the epidemiological setting to autocatalysis in the biochemical setting. We introduce a graph, called the ALT-graph (autocatalysis-leak-transition graph), which decomposes the contribution of each reaction to the Jacobian as autocatalytic, leak, or transition edges. We then present a systematic algorithm for splitting the ALT-graph, which is guaranteed to produce a valid reproduction number, $ρ(FV^{-1})$, while also decreasing computational complexity by lowering the rank of $FV^{-1}$. We apply the method to models of both biochemical reaction networks and infectious disease spread.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the next-generation matrix method from epidemiology to biochemical systems by reinterpreting "new infections" as autocatalysis, introducing an ALT-graph and a splitting algorithm that guarantees a valid reproduction number while reducing computational complexity.
AI.motivation: The next-generation matrix method, powerful for computing the basic reproduction number in epidemiological models, was recently extended to mathematical biochemistry for determining stability/instability of boundary steady states. However, challenges remain regarding when the method is mathematically valid, computationally tractable, and biologically meaningful in the biochemical setting.
AI.method: The authors shift the interpretation from new infections (epidemiology) to autocatalysis (biochemistry). They introduce the ALT-graph (autocatalysis-leak-transition graph), which decomposes each reaction's contribution to the Jacobian into autocatalytic, leak, or transition edges. They then present a systematic algorithm for splitting the ALT-graph.
AI.result: The splitting algorithm is guaranteed to produce a valid reproduction number ρ(FV⁻¹) while decreasing computational complexity by lowering the rank of FV⁻¹. The method is applied to models of both biochemical reaction networks and infectious disease spread.
AI.conclusion: By reinterpreting new infections as autocatalysis and using the ALT-graph with a systematic splitting algorithm, the next-generation matrix method becomes mathematically valid, computationally tractable, and biologically meaningful for biochemical reaction networks, while remaining applicable to infectious disease models.

title: pCoMole: Pareto-Constrained Molecule Editing with Discrete Flows
comment: Published at NeurIPS 2026. (Proceedings of the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, Sydney, Australia)
summary: Biomolecular therapeutics often start from known sequences and require targeted editing to improve multiple properties while satisfying hard biochemical and manufacturability constraints. However, existing generative methods do not jointly support multi-objective optimization, hard feasibility, and sequence editing in discrete, variable-length biological spaces. In this work, we introduce Pareto-Constrained Molecule Editing (pCoMole), a framework built on discrete flow matching that steers a pre-trained Edit Flow toward user-specified preferences while enforcing terminal feasibility. pCoMole defines a feasibility-gated terminal distribution using an augmented Tchebycheff utility and realizes the resulting preference tilt through a Doob-h transform of the underlying edit process. To make this construction practical, we approximate the required harmonic function using short Monte Carlo rollouts over candidate edits, yielding an efficient guided editor with provable preference consistency. We validate pCoMole by shrinking GFP while retaining fluorescence-related properties, shortening diverse Cas9 orthologs while preserving PAM specificity, and compressing peptide binders into short peptidomimetics that optimize seven drug-related properties under hard constraints. In wet lab testing, two 229-residue pCoMole-designed eGFP variants retained clear green fluorescence in BL21 cells after 10 deletions, with either one or two substitutions. Together, pCoMole enables constraint-aware, Pareto-aligned editing of biomolecular sequences in discrete, variable-length spaces.

AI.tldr: pCoMole is a discrete flow matching framework for multi-objective, constraint-aware editing of variable-length biomolecular sequences, steering a pre-trained Edit Flow via a Doob h-transform with Monte Carlo rollout approximation, validated on GFP, Cas9, and peptide binders.
AI.motivation: Biomolecular therapeutics require targeted sequence editing to improve multiple properties under hard biochemical and manufacturability constraints, but existing generative methods cannot jointly handle multi-objective optimization, hard feasibility, and editing in discrete, variable-length biological spaces.
AI.method: Built on discrete flow matching, pCoMole steers a pre-trained Edit Flow toward user preferences while enforcing terminal feasibility. It defines a feasibility-gated terminal distribution using an augmented Tchebycheff utility and realizes the preference tilt through a Doob h-transform of the edit process, approximating the harmonic function with short Monte Carlo rollouts over candidate edits.

In wet lab tests, two 229-residue eGFP variants retained clear green fluorescence in BL21 cells after 10 deletions with one or two substitutions.
AI.conclusion: pCoMole enables constraint-aware, Pareto-aligned editing of biomolecular sequences in discrete, variable-length spaces, providing an efficient guided editor with provable preference consistency.

title: Inferring Multi-Timescale Neural Dynamics with Switching Linear Dynamical Systems
summary: Neural activity often exhibits multiple timescales that can vary with behavioral states and task conditions. Identifying these timescales from neural recordings is important for better understanding neural computation and function. However, traditional approaches based on autocorrelation fitting are difficult to scale to high-dimensional population recordings and can become unreliable when neural dynamics change with behavior. State-space models have been a powerful framework for modeling high-dimensional neural population activity through latent dynamical systems, but standard formulations and inference methods do not explicitly account for multiple timescales and therefore do not guarantee accurate recovery of the underlying temporal structure. Motivated by these questions, we introduce the Multi-Timescale Switching Linear Dynamical System (MTS-SLDS), a framework for identifying regime-specific latent timescales from continuous or spiking neural observations. MTS-SLDS combines a multi-lag moment initialization, which captures temporal structure across multiple observation lags, with \textit{regime-conditioned} Laplace-EM inference, which reduces mixing of dynamical statistics across uncertain regimes. Characteristic timescales can then be extracted directly from the eigenvalues of the learned latent transition matrices. In synthetic and neural experiments with Gaussian and Poisson spike observations, MTS-SLDS accurately recovers timescales and switching structure over multiple datasets.

AI.tldr: MTS-SLDS is a switching linear dynamical system framework that identifies regime-specific latent timescales from neural recordings via multi-lag moment initialization and regime-conditioned Laplace-EM inference.
AI.motivation: Neural activity shows multiple timescales that vary with behavioral state and task. Autocorrelation-based methods don't scale to high-dimensional population recordings and become unreliable when dynamics change. Standard state-space models don't explicitly model multiple timescales, so they don't guarantee accurate recovery of temporal structure.
AI.method: MTS-SLDS combines a multi-lag moment initialization (captures temporal structure across multiple observation lags) with regime-conditioned Laplace-EM inference (reduces mixing of dynamical statistics across uncertain regimes). Timescales are extracted from eigenvalues of learned latent transition matrices. Supports Gaussian and Poisson (spiking) observations.
AI.result: In synthetic and neural experiments with Gaussian and Poisson spike observations, MTS-SLDS accurately recovers both timescales and switching structure across multiple datasets.
AI.conclusion: MTS-SLDS provides a scalable framework for identifying regime-specific latent timescales in high-dimensional neural population activity, enabling better understanding of neural computation and function.

title: RipplePLM: Structural and Property Decoupling for Protein Mutation Effect Generation
summary: Protein mutation effect generation asks a model to describe the functional consequence of a point mutation in natural language. Existing protein-to-text systems typically encode mutation information into undifferentiated representations, overlooking the organization of mutation-induced evidence across structural and biochemical factors. We propose RipplePLM, a mutation-aware generation framework centered on Direct-Distal Cross-Attention (DDCA). By constructing a residue-level Mutation Perturbation Field from pre-trained protein language models, DDCA leverages predicted contact maps to organize mutation representations into two pathways: the mutation site's immediate contact neighborhood and its multi-hop distal context. To complement this structural decomposition, we further introduce the Property Latent Chain (PLChain), which injects expert-guided supervision of biochemical property changes (e.g., thermostability and optimal pH) into the LLM hidden-state pathway through latent property tokens. On MutaDescribe, RipplePLM improves over mutation-specific baselines on temporal and structural splits; under a matched-backbone comparison, average structural-split ROUGE-L increases from {22.23} to {35.65}. Expert evaluation further shows a higher proportion of biologically accurate or relevant descriptions than the mutation-specific baseline. Additional ablations, representation diagnostics, and low-$N$ fitness regression experiments further support the effectiveness of the learned mutation-aware representations. Code: https://github.com/Lyu6PosHao/RipplePLM.

AI.tldr: RipplePLM is a mutation-aware protein-to-text generation framework that decomposes mutation effects into local and distal structural pathways plus biochemical property supervision, improving description quality on MutaDescribe.
AI.motivation: Existing protein-to-text systems encode mutation information into undifferentiated representations, ignoring how mutation-induced evidence is organized across structural and biochemical factors.
AI.method: Direct-Distal Cross-Attention (DDCA) builds a residue-level Mutation Perturbation Field from pre-trained protein language models and uses predicted contact maps to split representations into immediate contact neighborhood and multi-hop distal context. Property Latent Chain (PLChain) injects expert-guided biochemical property supervision (thermostability, optimal pH) via latent property tokens into the LLM hidden-state pathway.
AI.result: On MutaDescribe, RipplePLM beats mutation-specific baselines on temporal and structural splits; matched-backbone structural-split ROUGE-L rises from 22.23 to 35.65. Expert evaluation shows more biologically accurate/relevant descriptions than the baseline. Ablations, representation diagnostics, and low-N fitness regression further support the learned representations.
AI.conclusion: Organizing mutation effects into structural (local/distal) and biochemical pathways yields more effective mutation-aware representations for protein mutation effect generation.

title: A foundation for systematic analysis of transformers and RNNs for tractography
summary: Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a promising approach for improving diffusion MRI (dMRI) tractography, a task that remains limited by the intrinsic tension between local diffusion information and global anatomical plausibility. In this work, we systematically evaluate recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and Transformer models for iterative tractography, with particular attention to training strategies, input representations (including convolutional neural network (CNN)-based embeddings and end-of-sequence (EOS) tokens), and hyperparameter selection. We introduce a generation-validation phase enabling supervision at the streamline level during training, allowing supervision despite the mismatch between local loss functions and global streamline quality. Using the ISMRM2015 tractography challenge dataset, our models achieve the highest reported performance to date. Through controlled experiments, we quantify the impact of missing bundles, noisy or imperfect training streamlines, and invalid fibers in the training set. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of our best-performing models for in vivo data from the Tractoinferno database. Overall, our results highlight both the potential and the limits of sequence-based deep learning models such as Transformers and RNNs for tractography, and emphasize the need for improved phantoms and evaluation methods for in vivo validation. We provide takeaways and recommendations for future researchers training and validating sequence-based supervised methods for tractography.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates RNNs and Transformers for iterative dMRI tractography, introduces a generation-validation training phase for streamline-level supervision, achieves state-of-the-art results on the ISMRM2015 challenge, and analyzes robustness to imperfect training data while demonstrating in vivo applicability.
AI.motivation: dMRI tractography is limited by the tension between local diffusion information and global anatomical plausibility, and ML approaches—while promising—lack systematic study of training strategies, input representations, and hyperparameters.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of RNNs and Transformers for iterative tractography, examining training strategies, input representations (CNN-based embeddings, EOS tokens), and hyperparameters. A generation-validation phase enables streamline-level supervision despite the mismatch between local loss functions and global quality.
AI.result: Highest reported performance to date on the ISMRM2015 tractography challenge. Controlled experiments quantify effects of missing bundles, noisy/imperfect training streamlines, and invalid fibers. Best models applied to in vivo data from Tractoinferno.
AI.conclusion: Results highlight both potential and limits of sequence-based deep learning for tractography, emphasizing the need for improved phantoms and evaluation methods for in vivo validation, with takeaways and recommendations for future research.

title: Effective Resistance and Graph Neural Network Reliability in Tissue-Specific Interactomes
summary: Protein function annotation needs to know which predictions to distrust, not only what a model predicts. We ask whether tissue-specific interaction structure carries that information. Our candidate signal is effective resistance, used previously to relieve over-squashing by rewiring. Across 24 tissue-specific interactomes it is dominated by inverse degree, and the degeneration deepens as the co-expression filtered network grows, with a Spearman correlation of -0.955. The residual departure from that limit exceeds degree-preserving null graphs in all 24 networks. Controlling for predictive entropy, degree, annotation cardinality, local structure and feature-only difficulty, the residual explains additional per-node loss in 19 of 24 held-out networks once a permutation floor is subtracted, at every depth, and the effect strengthens monotonically with depth. The increment reaches 0.37% of the variance the controls leave unexplained, 5.6 times a permutation floor, against 1.5 times when the model is retrained in a degree-preserving null world. Selective prediction improves negligibly. The signal is reproducible; degree degeneration bounds it.

AI.tldr: Effective resistance in tissue-specific interactomes is dominated by inverse degree and its residual weakly predicts per-node loss in protein function annotation, but offers negligible selective-prediction gains.
AI.motivation: Protein function annotation requires knowing which predictions to distrust. The authors test whether tissue-specific interaction structure, specifically effective resistance, carries this uncertainty information.
AI.method: Analyzed 24 tissue-specific interactomes, measuring effective resistance and its residual departure from the inverse-degree limit versus degree-preserving null graphs. Controlled for predictive entropy, degree, annotation cardinality, local structure, and feature-only difficulty; compared against a permutation floor and a degree-preserving null retraining.
AI.result: Effective resistance is dominated by inverse degree (Spearman -0.955, worsening as the network grows). The residual exceeds null graphs in all 24 networks and explains additional per-node loss in 19 of 24 held-out networks at every depth, strengthening with depth. The increment reaches 0.37% of the variance controls leave unexplained (5.6x permutation floor), but selective prediction improves negligibly.
AI.conclusion: The effective-resistance signal is reproducible but bounded by degree degeneration, and it yields little practical selective-prediction improvement.
